items.title: Human Sacrifice Rituals in Ancient Britain
items.description:
When we picture human sacrifice in ancient Britain, the iconic, flaming Wicker Man often comes to mind. But how much of this is Roman propaganda, and what does the actual archaeology reveal? Tristan Hughes is joined by archaeologist Dr. Miles Russell to separate popular myth from gruesome reality. From perfectly preserved bog bodies in the north to mysterious grain pit burials down south, who were these victims and why did they die?

0:00 Introduction
2:00 Roman sources on Celtic human sacrifice
items.why_watch: Rather than recycling the dramatic Wicker Man imagery, this episode brings in archaeologist Dr. Miles Russell to ground the discussion in actual physical evidence — bog bodies, grain pit burials, and what Roman sources were likely exaggerating for political effect. It's a clean example of how archaeology quietly dismantles a pop-history narrative. Good for anyone who enjoys the 'here's what we actually know' style of history.

Can a black hole be made entirely from light? General relativity suggests that, in principle, concentrating enough
items.why_watch: The question sounds like clickbait but it isn't — this is a careful walkthrough of the kugelblitz concept, the theoretical construct where concentrated light forms a black hole through its own gravitational energy. Physics Explained earns its name by building up the relativistic logic step by step rather than just asserting the answer. At 35 minutes it asks for real attention, but the payoff is a genuine conceptual shift in how you think about mass and energy.

Why do we think space is curved near the sun? Because we see Mercury's orbit precess. We thought it was due to gravitational effects of other pla
items.why_watch: This video focuses on the 1919 Eddington solar eclipse expedition — the specific observational moment when light bending around the sun either confirmed or refuted general relativity — and explains why Newton's own gravity theory actually predicted a bending angle too, just the wrong one. FloatHeadPhysics is careful about the distinction between Einstein's 1911 prediction and his corrected 1915 value, which is a detail most popular accounts skip entirely. A tight 20 minutes that leaves you understanding why that expedition was genuinely decisive.

items.title: The Spacetime Metric
items.description:
In the (epic?) conclusion to our metric tensor trilogy, we dive a little deeper into the origins of the metric tensor in an attempt to bridge the conceptual gulf that lies between our ordinary, intuitive understanding of geometry and that abstracter comprehension of it required to master General Relativity's four-dimensional spacetime. Can we pave ourselves a path to clearer understanding in twenty minutes? Let us know in the comments.

Contents:
00:00 - Intro / Describing Distance
01:56 - Maps
items.why_watch: This is the third in Dialect's metric tensor series, and it's specifically tackling the conceptual leap from flat Euclidean geometry to the four-dimensional spacetime interval at the heart of general relativity. The channel's approach is to build intuition slowly rather than throw equations at you, so if you've bounced off GR before because the math felt unmoored from meaning, this is worth trying. Works best watched after the earlier two episodes, but the channel's production quality makes the backtrack worthwhile.

items.title: Miller effect made easy - Miller theorem - cascode amplifier
items.description: This video talks about the Miller effect which is very important when you want to analize the frequency beahvior of a circuit. The Miller effect is a powerfull approximation you use when a capacitance is in the gain path of a circuit. When the gain is negative the capacitance is magnified so this metod makes easy to find the dominant poles simply by inspection. We see an example of Miller effect in the common emitter configuration and we see also why the cascode configuration improves the bandwi
items.why_watch: The Miller effect is one of those topics that gets hand-waved in intro electronics courses but actually matters the moment you're designing anything that operates above audio frequencies. This eight-minute video shows specifically why a feedback capacitance gets multiplied by gain, and uses the cascode amplifier as a concrete example of engineering around it. Compact and precise — a useful reference even if you've seen the concept before.

news.title: Kid, London W1: ‘Fat, richness, sharpness, all in perfect balance’ – restaurant review
news.snippet: Our main course arrived heavy and somewhat intimidating, and left picked completely clean Earlier this month, a kind-of Turkish ocakbaşı opened on a corner in London’s Soho. The brains behind Kid are chef Sertaç Dirik and restaurateur David Carter, and I say “kind-of” because, yes, while it has a Turkish-influenced menu – sucuk with grilled peach, pide , börek , hummus, içli köfte with aged beef – and the whiff of live fire, nothing either of them does is ever remotely straightforward, hence the buzz around their new place. Carter founded Smokestak a decade ago in Shoreditch, a wild, Americana-tinged barbecue joint where, somehow, he made brisket in buns and peach cobbler old fashioneds London’s hottest ticket.
news.blurb: A Turkish ocakbaşı landing in Soho with the kind of fat-rich, sharply balanced cooking that leaves a plate — and a critic — utterly undone is exactly the restaurant story worth reading this week.
